description: Identifier of the interviewed household as assigned by the study team: the enumerator's initials, the survey date as day and month (2309 for 23 September 2026) and a running number per enumerator, for example AC-2309-001.
Code of the enumerator who conducted the interview, E1 to E5; the codes replace the mWater user names and are shared with guluswm_waste.
Date of the interview, between 23 and 26 September 2026.

Study area in which the household lives: Limo, Vanguard or Highland (Laroo-Pece Division), Kanyagoga, Pabbo Quarters or Goans Quarters (Bardege-Layibi Division). Only two interviews were completed in Highland. The raw file spells Pabbo Quarters as Pabwo Quarters in this sheet.
Administrative division of Gulu City in which the household lives: Bardege-Layibi or Laroo-Pece.
Number of people living in the household.
Whether the respondent is the head of the household (Yes or No).
Highest level of education of the household head, in rising order: None (no formal education), Primary, Secondary, Tertiary/vocational, University and above.
Main source of livelihood of the household: Trading/business, Casual labour, Salaried employment, Remittances/Donations or Other.
Monthly household income in Ugandan shillings, in six bands from None/no regular income to Above UGX 1,000,000.

Income class derived from income_band: Low (no regular income or below UGX 300,000), Middle (UGX 300,000 to 600,000) or High (above UGX 600,000). The proportions of these classes set the cut points of wealth_index_class.
Monthly household expenditure on basic needs in Ugandan shillings, in five bands from Below UGX 100,000 to Above UGX 1,000,000.
Main material of the walls of the dwelling: Mud/wattle, Unburnt bricks, Burnt bricks, unplastered, Burnt bricks, plastered or Other.
Main material of the roof of the dwelling: Grass thatch, Iron sheets (old/rusted), Iron sheets (new) or Tiles/permanent.
Whether the household has access to piped water (Yes or No).
Whether the household has access to electricity (Yes or No).
Types of waste the household generates, as named by the respondent: Food preparation waste, Food leftovers, Plastic, Paper, Glass or Other; several answers are separated by a semicolon.
Container in which the household stores its waste before disposal: Kavera (a polyethylene bag), Sack, Bucket or Bag; several answers are separated by a semicolon.

How the household disposes of its waste: Burning, Collected by service provider, Taken to collection point/skip, Backyard dumping, Rubbish pit, Roadside dumping, Open drain, Burying, Garden/compost or Other; several answers are separated by a semicolon.
Who collects the household's waste: City/Division Council, Private Operator, Informal Collector, Community Group, Self (household), No one or Other; asked of households with a collection arrangement.

Collection frequency the household would prefer: Daily, More than once a week, Three times a week, Twice a week, Weekly or Other; the answer Collection points every month was recorded under Other as an open answer.
Time of day the household considers best for collection: Morning, Day time, Evening, No specific time or Other.

Whether the household considers waste collection in its area reliable (Yes or No). The question was independent of waste_collector: some households whose waste is not collected take it to the municipal skips.

Main problem the household experiences from irregular collection: Dirty neighborhood, Unhealthy environment, Spread of diseases, Bad reputation of the area or Other; asked of households that call their service unreliable.
Whether the household considers the number of skips or collection points in its area enough (Yes or No).
Distance from the household to the nearest disposal point, in bands: Less than 50 Metres, 50 - 100 Metres, 200 - 300 Metres or More than 500 Metres.
Whether the household pays for waste collection (Yes or No).
Monthly fee the household pays for collection in Ugandan shillings, in five bands from Below UGX 1,000 to UGX 15,000 and above; asked of paying households.
How the household rates the fee it pays: Affordable, Manageable or Expensive; asked of paying households.

How the household pays for collection: Direct to City/Division Council, Through the landlord or Other. The question was shown to every household; for households that do not pay (pays_for_collection is No) the answer is not applicable, and for paying households Other covers channels not listed.

How often the household pays for collection: Daily, Whenever collected, Bi-weekly or Monthly. The question was shown to every household; for households that do not pay (pays_for_collection is No) the answer is not applicable.
Whether the household is willing to pay for an improved and regular collection service, or to pay more than now if it pays already (Yes or No).
Main reason for being willing to pay: Desire for a cleaner environment, Reduced risk of disease, Convenience/saves time, Improves property value or Other.

Main reason for not being willing to pay: Income is too low/irregular, Government/City should bear the cost, Already pay enough / rent includes it, Current service is unreliable so won't pay more, or Other.
Monthly amount the household is willing to pay in Ugandan shillings, in five bands from Below UGX 1,000 to UGX 15,000 and above; asked of willing households.
Payment structure the household prefers: Flat monthly fee, Pay-per-visit/per-collection, Pay-per-bag/per-bin collected, Included in property rent/rates or No preference.
Whether the household takes part in community clean-up exercises (Yes or No).
Whether the household has ever complained about solid waste management (Yes or No).
To whom the household complained: LCI Chairman (the chairperson of the Local Council I), Land Lord, City/Division Council, Private Operator or Other.
Whether the household receives information on solid waste management from the City (Yes or No).
Whether the household is aware of any solid waste management by-law (Yes or No).
Challenges of solid waste management in the area, coded by the study team from the respondent's answer; several codes are separated by a semicolon.
Improvements suggested by the respondent, coded by the study team from the free text answer; several codes are separated by a semicolon.

Post-stratification weight by division: the division's share of the population of Gulu City divided by its share of the sample. Bardege-Layibi 0.680 (population 93,848, sample 251) and Laroo-Pece 1.465 (population 139,423, sample 173), population figures from UBOS (2024).

Wealth index score computed by the study team: the first principal component of five standardised household indicators (roof of new iron sheets or tiles, plastered burnt brick walls, electricity, head with tertiary/vocational or university education, salaried employment as main livelihood); higher values mean wealthier. Missing for 18 households with a missing indicator.
Wealth class from wealth_index_score: households ranked by score and cut into Low, Middle and High in the proportions of income_class (63.4, 25.2 and 11.4 percent). Missing for 18 households.
Identifier of the characterisation record: CH, a batch number and a running number, for example CH-1001-001.
Code of the enumerator who recorded the measurement, one of the codes E1 to E5 shared with guluswm_survey.
Date on which the household's waste was weighed and sorted, between 1 and 3 October 2026, at the end of the storage period.
Study area of the household after correction by the study team: Limo, Vanguard, Highland, Kanyagoga, Pabbo Quarters or Goans Quarters.

Study area as recorded on the field form. The field kept the previous entry when two enumerators switched areas; the study team corrected 14 records against the enumerators' daily area logs and the field supervision records (see area).
Administrative division of Gulu City in which the household lives: Bardege-Layibi or Laroo-Pece.
Household number written on the field form and the bags, for example HH-01, used for field supervision; it restarts per enumerator and area and is not unique, record_id identifies the household.
Number of people living in the household.
Number of household members at home during the day.
Number of days over which the household stored its waste in the bags provided: 7 for every household but one in the test run, which stored for 14 days.
Occupants multiplied by days_stored, the denominator of the per capita generation rate.
Total weight of the household's waste as recorded in the field, in kilograms, before the correction of keying errors.
Sum of the weights of the 16 sorted fractions after the container deduction, in kilograms.

Total weight of the household's waste used for the generation rate, in kilograms: the recorded total, except for one keying error (CH-1001-012, grams entered as kilograms), where the sum of the sorted fractions is used.

Difference between the recorded total weight and the sum of the sorted fractions, as a percentage of the recorded total weight. Differences come from container weights, moisture loss and spillage during sorting; no record was excluded because of it.
Per capita waste generation rate in kilograms per person and day: weight_used_kg divided by person_days.
Per capita waste generation rate without the inert fines (sand, soil and stones), in kilograms per person and day: weight_used_kg minus inert_fines_kg, divided by person_days.

Whether the household is included in the averages of the study: the rule of at most 2.0 kilograms per person and day was applied to every record, and only one household exceeded it (No (outlier > 2.0)).
Weight of the empty 10 litre bucket used to measure the bulk density, in kilograms; one bucket was used and cleaned between households.
Weight of the 10 litre bucket filled loosely with the household's mixed waste before sorting, in kilograms; the mean of at least three weighings.
Bulk density of the loose waste in kilograms per cubic metre: the weight of waste in the 10 litre bucket divided by its volume.
Total weight deducted for the containers (weighing basins and bags) in which the fractions were weighed, in kilograms, summed over the fractions.

Container weight deducted from each fraction with a recorded weight, in kilograms. Where the raw fractions summed to more than the recorded total, the study team estimated it as the excess divided by the number of fractions weighed.
